accuracy.evidence: Facts checked against the DfE Year 1 measurement statement and the Gregorian calendar: 7 days a week, 12 months a year, months of 28 to 31 days, 365 days (366 in a leap year) which is 52 weeks plus 1 or 2 days. The lab's April has 30 days, giving 4 weeks and 2 days, and the text notes that UK/ISO weeks start on Monday while many US calendars start on Sunday.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips teachers report in Year 1 time work: the week 'ending' after Sunday, 5 days in a week from school days, mixing 7 days with 12 months or 52 weeks, swapping yesterday and tomorrow, counting today as the first day when finding a day 'in 3 days', and thinking a month is about a week long.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagcal builds a 7-slot week wheel and a 12-slot year wheel from shuffled name cards, turns a Today arrow that wraps from Sunday to Monday, draws numbered hop arcs from tomorrow onward, and fills a 7-column April calendar page with whole weeks before filling 12 month blocks. No other lab models cyclic calendar order or nesting of time units.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners first discover the fixed order by placing each next day, then see the cycle when the arrow passes Sunday, then learn counting on as hops that start at tomorrow, then repeat the order idea with months, and finally see that a 30-day month holds 4 whole weeks with 2 days over while 12 months make a year.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions: days in a week (5 is the tempting school-week answer), what follows Sunday (the week is over), months in a year (52 is tempting), and whether a week or month is longer (the same). Each is then contradicted on screen by the wheel, the wrapping arrow or the filled calendar.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions each route wrong answers through why() keyed to the slip: 'You counted Friday as 1' for the off-by-one, 'School may be 5 days, but the week has 7 days', 'Wednesday is tomorrow' for a yesterday/tomorrow swap, 'You skipped a month' for May after March, and the 52-weeks confusion.

readability.evidence: Kid text reads at FK grade 3.2 with short sentences and only the words a five-year-old needs: today, yesterday, tomorrow, week, month, year and the names themselves. Adult text reads at grade 9.2, quotes the Year 1 statement and lists the facts and errors in plain terms.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid sentence is a fact or a method (the order, the cycle, hop from tomorrow, 12 months), and every adult paragraph carries the curriculum statement, the numbers, the named mistakes or the lab steps. The content gate found no filler phrases and low overlap with Ordering Events in Time and Memory tricks.

mobile.evidence: Android 360 px screenshots in light and dark show both wheels, the hop arcs with numbered badges, the April grid and the 12 month blocks fully inside the canvas with no overlapping labels. Every action is a large button (day and month names, Yesterday, Tomorrow, Hop 1 day, Add a week), so no precise drag is needed.

accessibility.evidence: Every message updates the canvas aria-label and the polite live region, arrow buttons carry labels such as 'Go back one day', and chips use dark fills with white text that stay above 4.5:1 in both themes. axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations on desktop or iPhone in either theme.

sources: Department for Education (2013) Mathematics programmes of study: key stages 1 and 2, Year 1 Measurement: 'sequence events in chronological order using language' and 'recognise and use language relating to dates, including days of the week, weeks, months and years'; Year 2: 'know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day'
ISO 8601 (week numbering: weeks start on Monday) and the Gregorian calendar month lengths (28/29 to 31 days; 365 or 366 days in a year)
